title: The Numbers

narrative.text: The Finance Ministry smells like old paper and cold coffee. Vostane has been here since six this morning. You can tell by the number of cups on her desk.

Three people are already seated. Vostane at the head. Vyktor to her left. Marić standing by the window with his arms crossed, which means he has already read the numbers and already disagrees with something.
Chancellor. The preliminary budget assessment is complete. Before I present it I want to say one thing.

The numbers I am about to show you are worse than the projections you received during the campaign. Not because those projections were dishonest. Because the previous administration was dishonest with the people who made the projections.
They cooked the books. Say it plainly, Elara.
They misrepresented the structural deficit to the planning committee. I'll say it plainly when I have verified every figure. Until then I say: worse than projected.

monologue: Worse than projected. I ran on those projections. Twelve thousand people in Kravenstal voted for me on the strength of those projections. And now Vostane is telling me with the same tone she'd use to describe the weather that the ground has shifted under everything I promised. I need to understand exactly how bad before I decide anything.

choices.text: How bad? Give me the actual number.
If the books were cooked, I want to know who did it and why.
Gregor. You've seen these numbers. What's your read?

narrative.text: The structural deficit is negative sixty-five million Krone annually. The previous administration reported it as negative thirty-one. The gap is primarily in three areas — pension obligations they reclassified, infrastructure maintenance they deferred, and security apparatus costs they buried in a separate accounting line.
The honest number is negative sixty-five. We inherited negative sixty-five.
Which means every promise we made to the workers of Kravenstal—
Requires either new revenue, structural cuts, or deficit spending. There is no fourth option.
Silence. Vyktor is looking at the ceiling. Marić is looking at Vostane. Vostane is looking at you.

choices.text: New revenue. What are the options?
Structural cuts. What gets cut?
Deficit spending. For how long and at what cost?

narrative.text: The reclassification decisions ran through the Finance Ministry planning committee. Three signatures on each document. I have the names.
One of those names is currently a deputy minister in three other departments.
Which departments?
Trade. Transport. Regional Development.
Three departments where corruption would be nearly invisible and financially catastrophic. You file that thought away.

choices.text: I want those names on my desk by Friday. We'll deal with them after we stabilize the budget.
Remove them now. I won't govern with people who lied to us already.

narrative.text: Removing three deputy ministers in week three will be visible. The press will ask why. The answer will embarrass the previous administration — which is gone — but also raise questions about what else was misrepresented.
Which is either a problem or an opportunity depending on how you play it.
Play it as an opportunity. The workers want accountability. Give them accountability.
After we discuss the budget.

choices.text: Fine. Budget first. Then accountability.

narrative.text: My read. We promised the people of Kravenstal jobs and stability. We promised the teachers of Thornfeld their pensions. We promised the families of Aldenmoor that their children would have schools worth attending. Those promises don't disappear because the numbers are bad.
I know what Elara is going to recommend. I know what Vyktor is going to support. I want you to hear from me before they explain why the promises have to wait.
I haven't made a recommendation yet, Gregor.
You will.

choices.text: Noted, Gregor. Let me hear the numbers before I decide anything.
The promises matter. But I can't keep them on a broken budget. Let me hear what Vostane found.

narrative.text: Three viable options. Wealth tax on holdings above two million Krone — projected forty million annually, politically contested. Corporate rate increase on foreign-owned enterprises — projected twenty-two million, carries trade retaliation risk. Or resource extraction levy on the northern mining operations — projected eighteen million, affects Dravenhollow employment.
The wealth tax. Obviously the wealth tax.
The wealth tax will trigger a capital flight response. Vael Group alone has the leverage to—
Let Vael move his money. Let him explain to the Ashenmere press why he moved it.

choices.text: The wealth tax. We ran on redistribution. This is redistribution.
The corporate rate increase. It's defensible internationally and doesn't touch domestic capital.
A combination. Smaller wealth tax, smaller corporate increase. Split the political risk.

narrative.text: The three largest discretionary areas are infrastructure maintenance, social support programs, and the civil service wage bill. Cutting infrastructure saves twenty million but defers costs — the roads don't stop needing repair because we stop paying for it. Social support cuts save thirty million and produce immediate visible suffering. Civil service wages save fifteen million and produce a strike within forty-five days.
None of those.
Then we're discussing revenue or deficit spending.

choices.text: Infrastructure maintenance. The roads can wait. People can't.
I won't cut social programs. Show me the revenue options.

narrative.text: We can carry the deficit for approximately two years before the Krone comes under serious pressure. After that, the interest payments become structural and we enter a spiral. Deficit spending is a bridge, not a solution. The question is what we're bridging to.
Politically, two years is enough time to demonstrate results before the pressure becomes visible. If the reforms generate growth — and that's an if — we may not need the full two years.
Or we spend the two years keeping the promises we made, generate goodwill and political stability, and figure out the revenue question from a stronger position. Desperate governments make bad deals.

choices.text: Deficit spending for eighteen months while we build the revenue base. Controlled. Time-limited.
I won't start my government in debt. Find me revenue options.

narrative.text: The room is quiet. Three people waiting. The numbers are on the table. The promises are somewhere in the back of your mind. These two things are about to collide and there is no version of the next ten minutes where that doesn't hurt someone.
What is the government's budget direction, Chancellor?

final_budget_choice.monologue: Sixty-five million in the hole and a room full of people who each have a different answer. Vostane wants the numbers to add up. Marić wants the promises to mean something. Vyktor wants whatever keeps us in power long enough to do something with it. What do I want? I want all three. I'm about to find out which I can actually have.

choices.text: Prioritize welfare and social programs. The deficit is real but so are the people who voted for us. We find revenue while we spend.

reactions.text: The tension in his shoulders releases. All at once. Like something he'd been holding for weeks.
I'll adjust the projections. We'll need a revenue mechanism by month four or the Krone will notice.
He notes something in his folder. You cannot see what.

choices.text: Prioritize infrastructure investment. It creates jobs, generates long-term revenue, and the unions will accept delayed welfare expansion if they see construction employment numbers rise.

reactions.text: Correct. The multiplier effect on infrastructure is documented. I'll prepare the procurement framework.
The people in Kravenstal won't feel that for two years.

choices.text: Fiscal consolidation first. Cut what can be cut, raise what revenue we can, stabilize the Krone. I won't govern on a foundation that collapses in eighteen months.

reactions.text: Sound. The Krone will respond well. I'll have a consolidation schedule by Thursday.
He stands. He goes to the window. He doesn't ask permission.
The unions will want something in return. We should think about what we're prepared to offer.

choices.text: A balanced approach. Protect the core welfare programs, invest selectively in employment-generating infrastructure, find new revenue through the corporate levy. No one gets everything and no one gets nothing.

reactions.text: That is not a strategy. That is a position. I can work with it.
He starts to speak. He stops. He looks at the table.
